senses: A composite of fabrics (typically linen or paper fabric) using phenolic resins cured under pressure and high temperature to produce laminates.
A computer chip or similar hardware device used to modify the behaviour of a games console.
examples: Installing a new hard drive would require a modchip that can reprogram or bypass the hard drive lock.
The goal of this hack is to install a modchip into your Xbox.
Sony argued that the access code reader was a 'technological protection measure' and that the 'modchip' was a 'circumvention device'.

senses: Being the opposite or logical inverse of a familiar person, place, or situation.
ety: Variant of bizarre, equivalent to bizarre + -o; see that entry for more information. In the sense of “logical inverse”, derived via the comic book character Bizarro, an inverted version of Superman from a planet where “good” means “bad” and so on, and further popularized by "The Bizarro Jerry", a 1996 episode of the sitcom Seinfeld.
examples: Egypt is a Bizarro-Canaan, looking as Canaan might look seen through Alice's looking glass. It shows the Judeans how a country should not be run.

senses: near the anus
A person who has a schizotypal personality disorder
A male member of an assembly.
A member of the lower house of certain US state legislatures.
That hectors; intimidating or domineering.
examples: The types that started using “-maxxing” in earnest often did so with such hectoring self-seriousness that it was impossible not to parody.

senses: A decoration, especially on hats, made from twisted ribbon
examples: Harper's Magazine the crown decked with torsades of pearls

senses: A person who procures or obtains things
A person who procures customers for prostitutes.
ety: Inherited from Middle English procurour, from Anglo-Norman procurour and continental Old French procureor, from Latin prōcūrātor; by surface analysis, procure + er. Doublet of proctor and procurator.

senses: having the same pressures, masses, or densities
Designed to be collapsed, especially so as to be more compact when not in use.
A principal high-level cloud type appearing as a whitish veil, usually fibrous but sometimes smooth, which may totally cover the sky and which often produces halo phenomena.
ety: From cirro- + stratus, coined by the British chemist and amateur meteorologist Luke Howard (1772–1864): see the 1803 quotation.

senses: Not teachable.
A Jew or Muslim in Spain or Portugal who converted to Roman Catholicism under duress, particularly during the 14th and 15th centuries.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish converso. Doublet of converse.
examples: Guillermina Jasso, a sociology professor at New York University, said Angel was “evocative of the old converso practice of taking on very Christian surnames as a way of survival in a suspicious environment.”

senses: An animated cartoon published on the World Wide Web.
A kind of Korean comic that is published digitally for reading on a smartphone or computer.
ety: From Web + toon, dating from at least 2001 (see citations). For Korean comics, likely a re-borrowing of Korean 웹툰 (weptun), itself from the original sense.
examples: Have a webtoon! Elf Life: http://www.elflife.com
As Flash Webtoons and animated shorts have become more and more popular, a spate of tools have cropped up to facilitate their creation.
Ren & Stimpy creator John Kricfalusi used Flash animation to bring cartoons (sometimes called online cartoons or webtoons) to the Internet.

senses: One who, or that which, lights gas.
A deciduous timber-yielding tree native to West and West Central Tropical Africa, Nesogordonia papaverifera.
The wood of this tree.
ety: Borrowed from a certain Ghanaian vernacular name (compare Anyi danta, Sehwi danta).

senses: A cocktail with ingredients including orange juice and cream.
One who, or that which, sends an email.
examples: Pakistani police said on Tuesday that they have launched a hunt for an emailer whose threatening message to New Zealand cricketers nearly jeopardised their tour to Pakistan.
I also asked whether there had been any complaints (having been made aware by an emailer that he had put in a formal complaint to the website).

senses: A kind of roll.
ety: From Italian rotolo (“roll; rottol”). As a roll, from Late Latin rotulus (“little wheel”), from Latin rota (“wheel, rolling thing”) + -ulus (“-ule”, forming diminutives). As a unit of weight, from Arabic رُطْل (ruṭl), variant of classical رِطْل (riṭl), ultimately from Ancient Greek λίτρα (lítra).

senses: An instance of chiasmus.
ety: From New Latin chiasma, from Ancient Greek χῑ́ασμα (khī́asma), from χῑάζω (khīázō, “to mark with an X”).

examples: Building a cherishable memory is equally necessary in divorce situations.

senses: Designating a radar system that compares the received signal from a single radar pulse against itself in order to compare the signal as seen in multiple directions, polarizations, etc.

ety: Borrowed from Latin ōrdinālis, adjective formed from noun ōrdō (“order”), + adjective suffix -ālis.

senses: The branch of skincare dealing with protection against the effects of sunlight.
A small two-headed drum, used in Dominican merengue music, usually played by striking one side with a mallet and the other with the hand.
A large two-headed bass drum, used in Mexican banda and regional genres like tamborazo, usually played by striking both sides with a mallet (bolillo).
A wide two-headed drum used mainly in Colombian cumbia, played by striking both sides with heavy sticks (baquetas).
A posture in which one straddles something.
A voluntary raise made prior to receiving cards by the first player after the blinds.
A vertical mine-timber supporting a set.
A part of a harness placed on the back of a beast of burden (such as a horse or donkey) to carry the weight of a load.
ety: As a verb, attested since the 1560s. Most likely, an alteration of dialectal striddle. The noun is first attested in the 1610s.

senses: The adhesion of a liquid or gas on the surface of a solid material, forming a thin film on the surface.
ety: Borrowed from German Adsorption, from ad- + (Ab)sorption.

senses: Oatmeal mixed with boiling water or milk.
ety: From the Doric dialect of North East Scotland, from earlier browes, from Old French broez, nominative of broet (“stew, soup made from meat broth”) (French brouet) diminutive of breu, from Medieval Latin brodium, from Proto-Germanic *bruþą (“broth”). See broth.
examples: I had not far to seek for him: he stood waiting in the passage, for the cooling of his brose.

senses: Having micropores of a size less than 2 nanometres.

ety: From Middle English attender, attendere, equivalent to attend + -er.
examples: She was a very constant attender of First-day and week-day meetings, at the meeting places she belonged to
The great distance that some youth travel...is bound to play its part in the case of the borderline student who becomes an infrequent attender and finally drops out of school.
If there is no spiritual distinction between member and attender, the question is asked, Why have membership at all?
